lines.watchItem: Leading-edge wafer demand is booked far ahead of the plants: supply-chain sources put TSMC order visibility at 2030, its own tool demand runs at roughly 1.9 times what it projected in December 2025, and it still cannot meet demand while building about 20 plants at once. The exposure is construction labour and equipment delivery, not orders.

Advanced-packaging allocation is again named the binding limit on finished AI system availability, with lines quoted at 52 to 78 weeks against capacity of roughly 105,000 to 130,000 wafers a month by the fourth quarter of 2026. The same capacity is more than 85 percent pre-booked by three customers, with one holding about 60 percent of 2026 slots, so realizable revenue sits with a very short list of buyers.

Packaging work is starting to move to rival suppliers on wait times: Google has ordered more than 3 million units of Intel bridge packaging for 2028 delivery, and Samsung and Amkor routes are quoted at 26 to 39 weeks against 52 to 78 weeks. That is a share exposure in packaging rather than in wafers, and the answer so far is a bridge-style technology developed with Kinsus.

The leading-node customer base is broadening from merchant accelerator vendors toward buyer-designed silicon: the largest custom-chip designer guides its artificial-intelligence revenue from about $58 billion this year to $115 billion in 2027 and $230 billion in 2028, Microsoft is negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 of its own parts for 2027, OpenAI's first inference chip runs on a 3nm process, and Meta names TSMC for production. Wafer demand may hold while the names on the purchase orders change.

Price firmness runs the length of the chain right now: wafer price rises of 3 to 6 percent are reported for 2027, Samsung lifted advanced contract prices 10 to 15 percent, Nvidia is passing more than 15 percent into system prices from early next year, and one cloud provider is raising published hourly rental rates 17 to 21 percent from October. The watch-item is whether end buyers keep absorbing these steps.

Memory suppliers are taking a larger share of each AI server dollar: memory's share of AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach 57 percent in 2027 from 14 percent in 2025, while the leading accelerator vendor guides gross margin to 74.0 percent and names a floor of 71 to 72 percent on memory costs. Logic content competes for a shrinking slice of a growing bill of materials.

Second-source contract manufacturing is getting stronger rather than weaker: Intel's foundry revenue reached $5.8 billion, up 31 percent year over year, Samsung expects advanced processes to exceed half its foundry revenue, and a large model developer is in early talks with Samsung for a 2nm custom chip. Samsung still held only 7 percent of foundry revenue against more than 70 percent for TSMC in the first quarter of 2026.

Policy ties commercial terms to where plants are built: Washington is preparing semiconductor duties that would reach finished data-centre servers, with duty-free import allowances sized to each company's United States fabrication investment, against planned Arizona investment now totalling $265 billion. The exposure is that the tariff framework is still unwritten, with no rate or start date set.
